parts.description: A glossy red tomato with a rounded, slightly flattened fruit body and green fibrous calyx, leaves, and short stem. The surface appears smooth, thin-skinned, and moist with small natural speckles.
parts.reasoning: The object is a fresh tomato: a water-rich organic fruit with a nearly spherical/oblate body and lightweight leafy stem structure. A typical medium tomato has a diameter of about 55–70 mm and a mass of roughly 80–180 g; a representative value of 0.12 kg is appropriate for a single tomato of the shown size. Tomato bulk density is close to water but slightly lower due to internal air spaces and cellular tissue, so 950 kg/m^3 is a realistic rigid-body density estimate. The main fruit is soft and highly damped, so although this is modeled as a rigid body, contact behavior should use low restitution and optionally compliant contacts to approximate the non-bouncy, energy-absorbing response of a ripe tomato. The smooth waxy skin gives moderate friction on common clean surfaces: higher than glass/plastic because of slight tackiness and moisture, but lower than rubber. Static friction is estimated at 0.55 and dynamic friction at 0.42. Restitution is set low at 0.12 because a tomato deforms internally and dissipates impact energy rather than bouncing. For collision geometry, the best practical Isaac Sim representation is convex decomposition: one near-spherical or ellipsoidal convex part for the fruit body plus simplified convex hulls/capsules for the calyx leaves and stem if they need physical contact. If only gross manipulation/contact is required, a sphere or ellipsoid approximation for the body alone is faster and usually more stable; however, convex decomposition better preserves the protruding green top. A full triangle mesh collider is not recommended for a dynamic rigid body in PhysX unless converted to SDF or simplified, and SDF would be unnecessarily expensive for most tomato interactions. Contact offset of about 2 mm is suitable for a small organic object in meter units, providing stable contact generation without visibly floating. Rest offset is kept at 0 so the collider aligns closely with the visible mesh. CCD is recommended because the tomato is small and can be dropped or thrown; it helps prevent tunneling through thin surfaces. Initial velocity is zero, with normal Earth gravity. For non-deformable approximation of a soft fruit, compliant contacts can be enabled with moderate stiffness and high damping to reduce unrealistic hard impacts. Suggested solver settings would use 60–120 Hz simulation; 120 Hz is preferable for grasping or impacts with small objects. Sleep/hibernation should be allowed after motion settles to improve performance, with a low sleep threshold because the mass is small; avoid excessive contact offsets or overly detailed leaf colliders that can cause jitter.
